title: Youth mental health and digital life
text:
This is a brutally chilling article on youth mental health epidemic in America as potentially caused by our schools!  This has far-ranging indictment of our schools, parents, health system, and has implications on our politics and public policy. 
 
Here is a brief, clean, and structured response: a short thesis summary, a data-based counterargument, and a practical approach to the school-related mental-health problem.

1. Central Thesis (Brief Summary)

The article argues that the rapid rise in childhood mental-health diagnoses—ADHD, autism, anxiety, depression—cannot be understood without examining school itself. Modern education has become high-pressure, metrics-driven, standardized, and developmentally mismatched to children’s needs. As demands increased (testing, early reading, reduced recess, packed schedules), more children struggled to “fit the track,” leading parents, teachers, and systems to rely increasingly on psychiatric labels to secure support. Essentially, schools have changed faster than children, and diagnoses are partly a systemic response—not necessarily an explosion of pathology.

2. Data-Based Counterargument

While school stress likely contributes, the dramatic rise in diagnoses is not fully explained by schooling alone. Several data-supported trends point elsewhere:

A. Diagnostic Expansion & Improved Detection

Autism criteria broadened significantly in 1994 and 2013, shifting many children from “learning disability,” “speech delay,” or “behavior problem” categories into autism.

CDC data shows the largest increases in mild, functional autism, not severe cases—consistent with better screening, not necessarily increased incidence.

B. Greater Awareness and Lower Stigma

Surveys (Pew, CDC) show a 300% increase since the 1990s in parents seeking behavioral evaluations.

Anxiety and depression are discussed more openly, leading to more help-seeking and fewer untreated cases.

C. Biological and Environmental Contributors

Research documents rising rates of:

Preterm birth (strongly correlated with ADHD/anxiety)

Maternal stress and prenatal exposure to pollutants

Sleep deprivation and screen-based light exposure, both affecting mood regulation

These are independent of schooling.

D. Cross-national comparisons complicate the thesis

Countries with far less test-based schooling (e.g., UK, Canada, Australia) report similar surges in youth anxiety and depression.

Scandinavian nations with lighter academic pressure still report rising autism and ADHD diagnoses.

Implication:
School stress is a factor, but not the primary driver; broader technological, diagnostic, and environmental changes are at work.

3. A Practical Approach to the School-Mental-Health Problem

A balanced solution acknowledges that schools magnify stress, but the broader ecosystem (screens, family dynamics, diagnostic culture) also matters. A viable approach includes:

A. Restore Developmentally Appropriate Schooling

Reintroduce mandatory recess and unstructured play (shown to reduce ADHD-like behavior by 30â40%).

Reduce early academic push (e.g., delay formal reading instruction to age 6â7, aligned with child-development norms).

Adopt block schedules to lower cognitive load.

B. Shift from Punitive Metrics to Whole-Child Metrics

Replace test-driven accountability with growth-based assessments.

Encourage project-based learning, shown to reduce anxiety and improve engagement.

C. Universal School Design for All Children (not only diagnosed ones)

Rather than forcing diagnoses to unlock accommodations:

Provide movement-friendly classrooms (standing desks, sensory/movement breaks).

Train teachers in neurodiversity-informed practices.

Implement tiered supports so mild struggles don’t require a medical label.

D. Improve the Child’s Non-School Environment

Enforce healthy screen-time norms (especially evenings).

Educate families on sleep hygiene, a strong protective factor for mood.

Connect schools to community-based counselors for early intervention.

E. Better Data and Better Discipline Around Diagnoses

Encourage second opinions and functional assessments before assigning lifelong labels.

Use behavioral supports first, medication only when clearly beneficial.

In One Sentence

The central thesis is that schools—not children—have changed, driving a surge in diagnoses; but a counterargument based on data shows that broader diagnostic, technological, and developmental trends play equally large roles, and a balanced solution involves redesigning both school environments and supportive systems without medicalizing every child.

title: Notes on Being a Man
text:
I just completed an audiobook that I wish to strongly endorse!  This is especially true for anyone with kids, boys in particular!  Galloway is a 60+ year old NYU business school prof who made money being a serial entrepreneur (sold L2, Inc, a marketing communications firm in 2017 for $130M) and is a skilled public speaker with podcasts, etc. 

Scott Galloway’s Notes on Being a Man is a sharp, candid, and often vulnerable reflection on what modern masculinity should look like—and what happens when men fail to evolve. Drawing from his own life story—growing up with financial insecurity, navigating ambition, failures, divorce, parenting, aging, and professional reinvention—Galloway offers a blend of memoir, social commentary, and tough-love guidance.

At the heart of the book is the thesis that traditional models of masculinity are obsolete, and that many men today suffer from loneliness, lack of purpose, and poor emotional skills. Galloway argues that being a good man is less about dominance, stoicism, or material success, and more about responsibility, emotional openness, discipline, and connection.

He explores themes such as:

The danger of isolation, especially among young men who lack mentors or meaningful relationships.

The importance of competence and resilience, not as performance, but as tools to support others.

Ambition and humility, and the paradox that real confidence comes from acknowledging your weaknesses.

Love and partnership, where he stresses loyalty, communication, and showing up consistently.

Fatherhood, and how being a present, emotionally intelligent parent is one of the highest callings of manhood.

Aging and mortality, including letting go of ego, accepting limitations, and shifting from “warrior” to “sage.”

Throughout, Galloway mixes harsh truths with humor and autobiographical honesty—admitting his own mistakes in relationships, work, and self-image. His overarching message: Manhood should be earned, not inherited, and it requires continuous growth, self-awareness, and service to others.

The book ultimately serves as both a critique of outdated masculine norms and a blueprint for healthier, more grounded male identity in the 21st century.

title: 1929 and the lessons of a market crash
text:
Just read this chilling and instructive book by Andrew Ross Sorkin about the 1929 market crash.  Book focused on the period between 1928 - 1934, at the end of the "roaring 1920s".

Sorkin emphasizes people, incentives and personality rather than purely economic charts. He writes that he wanted to know: “what they were saying to one another, what the motivations were, what the incentives were.” 

The book underlines how credit and leverage were central in the boom years (banks' lending to speculators, margin purchases) and how many of the bank/industry titans either enabled or actively promoted that.

The narrative links the bubble not just to wild speculation but to structural features: the weak regulatory state, the interlocking roles of industry/finance/politics, banking’s dominance, and the illusion that “this time is different.” 

What emerges are critical banking reforms:

1. Forced separation in the banking industry between commercial lending arm and investment arm
2, Establishment of the FDIC to form a gov't backstop for banks and protect consumer confidence and present "runs on the bank"
3. Strengthening of the SEC and Federal Reserve

Parallels to 2025 and AI bubble? I really did not see much there!

The book goes into great detail about specific characters in the: 

A. Hoover Administration & Government Players

1. Herbert Hoover — President of the United States
Presided over the economy during the crash, initially minimizing the collapse and relying on voluntary cooperation rather than aggressive federal action.

2. Andrew W. Mellon — Secretary of the Treasury
Powerful financier-turned-Treasury Secretary whose laissez-faire, anti-intervention philosophy shaped the government’s restrained early response to the crash.

3. Carter Glass — U.S. Senator (later architect of GlassâSteagall)
One of the few political voices warning about speculative excess, representing the push for tougher regulation against dominant banks.

4. Roy A. Young — Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board
The cautious Fed leader who struggled to rein in speculation and faced open defiance from major banks when trying to tighten margin lending.

5. Eugene Meyer — Governor of the Federal Reserve Board (and later Fed Chairman)
Key internal Fed figure who argued for stronger action but faced political and institutional resistance.

B. Major Bankers & Wall Street Titans

6. Charles E. Mitchell — Head of National City Bank (Citigroup predecessor)
Perhaps the book’s greatest villain: aggressively fueled margin lending, openly undermined the Fed, and helped inflate the bubble.

7. Thomas W. Lamont — Senior Partner, J.P. Morgan & Co.
A central character whose diaries form a foundation of the book; attempted to coordinate rescues on Black Thursday but ultimately could not stop the collapse.

8. Albert Wiggin — Chairman of Chase National Bank
A powerful banker later revealed to have shorted his own bank’s stock during the crash, embodying conflicts of interest and insider manipulation.

9. Ben Smith & William Durant — Ad-hoc “market stabilizers”
Two wealthy figures who tried to prop up the market after the initial crash by buying up shares, illustrating the fragile efforts to restore confidence.

10. Richard Whitney — Vice President of the NYSE
Famous for his dramatic purchase of U.S. Steel shares on Black Thursday to halt panic selling, later disgraced for embezzlement.

C. Industry Titans, Corporate Figures & Speculative Actors
11. John J. Raskob — DuPont/GM executive; Democratic Party power broker
A symbol of 1920s optimism who encouraged ordinary Americans to buy stocks and used his corporate/political power to promote the bull-market ethos.

12. Jesse Livermore — Legendary speculator
The era’s most famous trader, who initially profited by shorting the market but became a tragic emblem of emotional and financial overreach.

13. William C. Durant — Founder of General Motors; serial market gambler
A wildly charismatic industrialist whose attempts to corner stocks exemplified the era’s reckless belief that the boom could be controlled by a few strong hands.

14. Arthur Wiesenberger — Market analyst and promoter
One of the public voices fanning retail investor enthusiasms, reflecting how media and newsletters contributed to speculative fever.

15. Evangeline Adams — Celebrity astrologer who advised investors

title: Ken Burns and The American Revolution
text:
Watched the first episode of this six-part series on PBS (total 12 hours streaming). Again, masterful take on American history: music, photography, illustrations, comments by historians, and voice overs from actors. The series takes perspectives from multiple stakeholders.  More vividly than what I recall from high school! 
I assume this "version" was approved by Brendan Carr!

What is striking is the amount of time devoted to actual tactics of battlefield warfare, with troop movements, etc.  So many of the battles occurred in the tri-state areas of NY, NJ, and PA along the waterways (after the initial Lexington/Concord/Boston battle).  The series was so captivating without actual "war footage" (that modern audiences take for granted in movies), but the battles were explained and dramatized using still drawings, portraits, etc. And what is so cool are the battlefields were so local to where we live near Philadelphia!

title: The Golden Road and ancient India
text:
I just listened to The Golden Road (William Dalrymple) on Spotify as a "free" audiobook, which allows 15 hours per month for books (this book was about 16 hours?). The print version has many historical maps and color photos, which would have been quite helpful (the book is on back order).

I found the book to be a gripping story told by an ardent storyteller who also is a researcher. The narrative takes a perspective that is little known in the West.

Dalrymple’s central claim is that, between roughly 250 BCE and ~1200 CE (or somewhat later), the Indian subcontinent was the fulcrum of a vast civilizational and economic sphere—a “Golden Road” of ideas, goods, and influences—spreading out across Eurasia, from the Roman world in the west to China, Korea, and Japan in the east. He argues that Indian learning, culture, religion (especially Buddhism and Hinduism), mathematics, science, art, architecture and trade had a much larger and earlier global impact than is often acknowledged. 

In his words (paraphrased): India was not just a passive recipient of external influences, but an active generator and exporter of culture and knowledge, connected through maritime and overland networks (monsoon-winds, maritime trade) that knit together a vast “Indosphere”. 

Here are the key supporting arguments and themes:

Maritime trade and the “Golden Road”

Dalrymple emphasizes how India’s geographical position, aided by monsoon winds, gave it access to maritime trade routes across the Indian Ocean, Red Sea, and beyond. 

He argues that this maritime trade preceded, and in many ways superseded, the overland “Silk Road” routes (which tend to dominate popular imagination). 

Example: trade from India into Roman Egypt and the Roman empire, bringing pepper, textiles, gemstones, luxury goods; the Roman writer Pliny called India “the sink of the world’s most precious metals”. 

The “Indosphere” and cultural influence

Dalrymple coins or uses the term “Indosphere” to describe the cultural-geographical zone influenced by India’s ideas, religions and languages (especially Sanskrit, Indian art/architecture, Buddhism, Hinduism) stretching across South Asia into Southeast Asia, East Asia and beyond. 

He highlights the spread of Buddhism from India into China, Korea, Japan; the adoption of Indian/Hindu cultural forms in Southeast Asia (temples, scripts, art) such as at Angkor Wat (Cambodia) or Borobudur (Indonesia). 

He emphasizes that many of these influences were non-coercive: the spread was by trade, pilgrimage, ideas — “soft power” — rather than by large-scale military conquest. 

Science, mathematics, knowledge transmission

Dalrymple argues that India made major contributions to mathematics (zero, the decimal system, algebra, trigonometry), astronomy (earth’s rotation, planetary motion) and that these ideas travelled from India to the Islamic world and then to Europe. 

For instance, he mentions the Indian mathematician Aryabhata and Brahmagupta, and the transmission of Indian numerals via the Abbasid world to the West (via figures like Fibonacci) in later centuries. 

Decline and transition

He argues that this period of Indian centrality eventually declines due to changing geopolitical and trade conditions: e.g., the arrival of Persianized Turkic empires, disruption of trade routes, the rise of Chinese and Central Asian power, and eventually the dominance of other networks. 

He also suggests that the reason this “Golden Road” narrative is under-emphasized in standard histories is due to biases (colonial historiography, Western-centric narratives, focus on Europe/China rather than India’s outward influence). 
History Reclaimed

Modern relevance

Dalrymple uses this history to reflect on how the past might inform present-day India and global dynamics: e.g., the idea of interconnectedness, soft power, cultural flows, and how India might reclaim or rediscover aspects of this legacy.

He argues that this maritime trade preceded, and in many ways superseded, the overland “Silk Road” routes (which tend to dominate popular imagination). 

Example: trade from India into Roman Egypt and the Roman empire, bringing pepper, textiles, gemstones, luxury goods; the Roman writer Pliny called India “the sink of the world’s most precious metals”. 

The “Indosphere” and cultural influence

Dalrymple coins or uses the term “Indosphere” to describe the cultural-geographical zone influenced by India’s ideas, religions and languages (especially Sanskrit, Indian art/architecture, Buddhism, Hinduism) stretching across South Asia into Southeast Asia, East Asia and beyond. 

He highlights the spread of Buddhism from India into China, Korea, Japan; the adoption of Indian/Hindu cultural forms in Southeast Asia (temples, scripts, art) such as at Angkor Wat (Cambodia) or Borobudur (Indonesia). 

He emphasizes that many of these influences were non-coercive: the spread was by trade, pilgrimage, ideas — “soft power” — rather than by large-scale military conquest. 

Science, mathematics, knowledge transmission

Dalrymple argues that India made major contributions to mathematics (zero, the decimal system, algebra, trigonometry), astronomy (earth’s rotation, planetary motion) and that these ideas travelled from India to the Islamic world and then to Europe. 

For instance, he mentions the Indian mathematician Aryabhata and Brahmagupta, and the transmission of Indian numerals via the Abbasid world to the West (via figures like Fibonacci) in later centuries. 

Decline and transition

He argues that this period of Indian centrality eventually declines due to changing geopolitical and trade conditions: e.g., the arrival of Persianized Turkic empires, disruption of trade routes, the rise of Chinese and Central Asian power, and eventually the dominance of other networks. 

He also suggests that the reason this “Golden Road” narrative is under-emphasized in standard histories is due to biases (colonial historiography, Western-centric narratives, focus on Europe/China rather than India’s outward influence). 
History Reclaimed

Modern relevance

Dalrymple uses this history to reflect on how the past might inform present-day India and global dynamics: e.g., the idea of interconnectedness, soft power, cultural flows, and how India might reclaim or rediscover aspects of this legacy.

title: Revisiting The Screwtape Letters
text:
I just re-read CS Lewis' Screwtape Letters!  I find this book to be so creative and hilarious (putting the deeper themes aside!).  This has kindled some interesting ideas for a project (more to follow).

The central thesis of The Screwtape Letters is that human beings are constantly subject to spiritual warfare, where subtle temptations and distractions orchestrated by demonic forces can lead them away from faith, virtue, and a relationship with God. 

The Screwtape Letters is structured as a series of 31 letters written by Screwtape, a senior demon, to his nephew Wormwood, a junior tempter. The epistolary format provides a one-sided correspondence, with each letter offering advice on how Wormwood should manipulate his human “patient” to secure his damnation. The letters are arranged chronologically, following the patient’s spiritual journey through various life events, such as falling in love, experiencing wartime anxiety, and grappling with faith.

One can contextualize other topics on similar grounds?

Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast, Ireland, in 1898 to a family of avid readers. Lewis, too, was soon immersed in literature: He started reading at just 3 years old, and by age 5, he had begun writing stories about a fantasy land populated by “dressed animals.”

 
Years later, a 19-year-old Lewis served in World War I with the Somerset Light Infantry. He experienced trench warfare on the front line in the Somme, the horrors of which he carried with him for the rest of his life.
Lewis first met J.R.R. Tolkien in 1926, and the two men developed a lifelong friendship. Lewis, who had become an atheist early in life, found his way back to theism and Christianity under Tolkien’s guidance. Tolkien, meanwhile, openly credited Lewis as a major source of creative encouragement: “Only from him,” wrote Tolkien, “did I ever get the idea that my âstuff’ could be more than a private hobby. But for his interest and unceasing eagerness for more I should never have brought The Lord of the Rings to a conclusion.”
Lewis himself was a prolific writer of both fiction and nonfiction. The latter included books and essays of Christian apologetics in which he passionately promotes and defends Christianity. Christian themes are also highly prevalent in his works of popular fiction, which include The Screwtape Letters, The Space Trilogy, and, most famously, The Chronicles of Narnia.
Here are 18 quotes from C.S. Lewis’ letters, essays, and literary works, covering a range of subjects from reading and writing to the importance of friendship.
Friendship is the greatest of worldly goods. Certainly to me it is the chief happiness of life. If I had to give a piece of advice to a young man about a place to live, I think I should say, “sacrifice almost everything to live where you can be near your friends.”

You can’t get a cup of tea large enough or a book long enough to suit me.

Everyone thinks forgiveness is a lovely idea, until they have something to forgive.

We have trained [people] to think of the Future as a promised land which favoured heroes attain — not as something which everyone reaches at the rate of sixty minutes an hour, whatever he does, whoever he is.

I do not think the forest would be so bright, nor the water so warm, nor love so sweet, if there were no danger in the lakes.

We all want progress. But â¦ if you are on the wrong road, progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road; and in that case, the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man.

No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear.

When I was ten I read fairy tales in secret and would have been ashamed if I had been found doing so. Now that I am fifty I read them openly. When I became a man I put away childish things, including the fear of childishness and the desire to be very grown up.

You never know how much you really believe anything until its truth or falsehood becomes a matter of life and death to you.

The value of the myth is that it takes all the things we know and restores to them the rich significance which has been hidden by the “veil of familiarity.”

A children’s story which is enjoyed only by children is a bad children’s story. The good ones last. A waltz which you can like only when you are waltzing is a bad waltz.

The task of the modern educator is not to cut down jungles but to irrigate deserts.

title: Debate and political persuasion
text:
Charlie Kirk (may he RIP) was indeed a good debater (without a formal college degree). His audiences were typically undergrad students in smaller colleges in the south and west, where he was the older, more experienced guy with the microphone with a following who managed the conversation. To his credit, he put himself out there to be "challenged" and "prove me wrong." 

This review in the NY Times explores the debating techniques that helped him seemingly "win." These strategies are worth paying attention to as you listen to "influencers" from a variety of domains. 
1. Hyperbole and go-to quips; make an outlandish statement and have an extreme example on hand.
2. Be Engaging — and subduing — the audience; communicate to the audience and ask them to observe, as well as the person asking the question.
3. Use Nazi analogies and playing to the crowd; these analogies are the most heinous acts that we all agree on.
4. Citing statistics with confidence (whether true or not); article notes verifiable misstatements.
5. Use Unprovable generalizations; for example, make some categorically unprovable assertions about the differences between women and men, as a starting point.
6. Debate skills honed over time.

In one form or another, we all engage in debate in our lives, may or may not be over politics. But being a good debater is a practiced skill, and at the least being aware of techniques used are important to help formulate your position.

Interestingly, Ezra Klein’s guest this week is Ta-Nehisi Coates, and they debate and discuss how to talk about Charie Kirk, who was brutally murdered by an unhinged person, but who also pedaled very divisive and hateful ideology. And the politics of our times.

title: The Supreme Court and constitutional interpretation
text:
This week's podcast was with Kate Shaw, legal scholar at Univ of Penn, on helping to understand the recent decisions by the Supreme Court.  I learned about the traditional "merit docket" vs. the "shadow docket." This was new concept for me, and it is important for the public to understand. This opaque system is facilitating strengthening the executive branch.

What is the Shadow Docket?

The Supreme Court's shadow docket, also known as the emergency docket, refers to a process where the Court issues rulings on urgent applications—such as stays, injunctions, or other interim orders—without the full procedural steps typically associated with its decision-making. These decisions are often made quickly, on compressed timelines, and may lack extensive briefing from parties, oral arguments, amicus curiae (friend-of-the-court) briefs, or detailed, signed opinions explaining the rationale. Instead, outcomes are frequently announced in brief, unsigned orders that provide little to no reasoning, even when they have significant real-world impacts. The term "shadow docket" was popularized by legal scholar William Baude in 2015 to highlight this less visible side of the Court's work, which contrasts with the more public and structured handling of cases.

The Alternative: The Merits Docket

In contrast, the merits docket (or regular docket) represents the Court's standard process for deciding cases. Here, cases undergo a thorough review: parties submit detailed briefs, the Court often hears oral arguments, amicus briefs from interested third parties are common, and justices have ample time for deliberation. Decisions are typically issued as signed opinions, with explanations of the legal reasoning, and may include concurrences or dissents. This process adheres to established appellate standards, such as evaluating preliminary injunctions based on factors like "abuse of discretion" or "irreparable injury." The merits docket is designed for cases that warrant full consideration, often setting binding precedents that guide lower courts and the public.

Implications of the Shadow Docket vs. the Merits Docket

The shadow docket's implications stem from its speed and opacity, which can enable rapid interventions in high-stakes issues but at the cost of transparency and accountability. Proponents argue it allows the Court to address emergencies efficiently, such as halting potentially unlawful actions while fuller litigation proceeds. However, critics contend it undermines the Court's legitimacy by allowing major policy shifts—on topics like immigration, executive power, or civil rights—without public explanation or robust debate, potentially leading to weaker legal reasoning due to rushed processes and incomplete records. This can erode public trust, as the Court appears less like a deliberative body and more like a partisan actor, especially when rulings align with political agendas without justification.

By comparison, the merits docket fosters greater procedural regularity and public confidence through its transparency, helping the Court fulfill its role in educating the public on legal principles and maintaining non-partisan credibility. It allows for more developed factual records and comprehensive analysis, reducing the risk of premature or poorly substantiated decisions. However, it is slower, which can delay resolution in time-sensitive matters. The shadow docket's rise, particularly post-COVID and in politically charged contexts, has amplified debates about whether the Court is over relying on it for substantive rulings that effectively become precedents without the merits docket's safeguards.

Recent Decisions with Examples

The shadow docket has been prominently used in recent years for cases involving executive actions, especially during the 2024-25 term amid ambitious policies. Below are examples from 2023-2025, illustrating how shadow rulings have enabled quick, impactful changes compared to what a merits docket process might entail:

Trump v. Wilcox (May 22, 2025): The Court overturned a preliminary injunction blocking the removal of commissioners from the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) and Merit Systems Protection Board, despite laws requiring "cause" for such firings. This unsigned order allowed immediate executive action without explanation, potentially overriding long-standing precedents like Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935). On the merits docket, this might have involved full arguments on separation of powers, leading to a more reasoned opinion.

Social Security Administration v. American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees (June 6, 2025): The Court paused an injunction preventing Department of Government Efficiency team members from accessing SSA records. This brief ruling facilitated administrative changes without detailing the legal basis, contrasting with a merits review that could have explored privacy and authority issues in depth.

Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. (June 23 and July 3, 2025): In two related orders, the Court lifted restrictions on deportations to unlisted countries, including South Sudan, allowing them to proceed immediately. These decisions had direct humanitarian impacts but lacked any rationale, raising transparency concerns; a merits docket approach might have included oral arguments on international law and due process.

Trump v. American Federation of Government Employees (July 8, 2025): The Court stayed an injunction against mass firings in federal agencies, enabling the dismissal of thousands of workers. This shadow ruling was terse and unsigned, potentially skirting appellate standards—unlike a merits case, which could have produced dissents and concurrences clarifying the implications for civil service protections.

McMahon v. New York (July 14, 2025): The Court granted a stay on a district court injunction blocking the winding down of the Department of Education, allowing steps toward its dismantling. The four-sentence order provided no substantive reasoning, prompting a 19-page dissent from Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson on separation-of-powers threats. A merits docket handling might have resulted in a fully argued decision with broader legal guidance.

Trump v. Boyle (July 23, 2025): The Court overturned an injunction protecting Consumer Product Safety Commission members from removal without cause. This emergency order continued a pattern of favoring executive firings without explanation, highlighting the shadow docket's role in enabling swift policy shifts that could face more scrutiny on the merits docket.

These examples, many tied to Trump administration actions in 2025, show how the shadow docket can resolve disputes effectively in the government's favor with minimal oversight, while the merits docket would likely demand more accountability and potentially different outcomes through deliberation. Critics argue this trend amplifies the docket's "shadowy" nature, urging reforms for greater transparency.

title: Flu and COVID vaccination guidance
text:
Good common-sense summary of guidelines for flu and covid shots for Fall 2025; everyone should get the flu shot and over 65 gets both flu and covid, any time before Halloween is ok.

CDC Recommendation for Flu Shot in 2025

The CDC recommends that all individuals aged 6 months and older receive a flu vaccine each season. For the 2025-2026 flu season, the CDC has updated its recommendations to include trivalent vaccines that are free of thimerosal as a preservative. The vaccines will protect against three main groups of circulating seasonal influenza Type A and B viruses: an A (H1N1) virus, an A (H3N2) virus, and a B/Victoria lineage virus. The FDA has approved FluMist and Flublok for self- or caregiver administration, respectively. The vaccine supply for the U.S. is projected to be as many as 154 million doses.

What is the evidence that flu shots benefit healthy adults?

Current guidelines from organizations like the CDC recommend annual flu vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and older, including young healthy adults, primarily to reduce the risk of influenza infection, prevent severe outcomes, limit transmission to vulnerable groups, and minimize societal disruptions like missed work.  Evidence specifically for benefits in young healthy adults (typically defined as those aged 16-65 without underlying conditions) comes from randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and observational data, showing modest but measurable effects that vary by vaccine match to circulating strains, flu season intensity, and outcome measured. 

Key findings include:

Reduction in Confirmed Influenza Cases
â¢  A Cochrane systematic review of 52 trials involving over 80,000 healthy adults found that inactivated flu vaccines provide about 59% efficacy against lab-confirmed influenza, reducing the risk from approximately 2.3% in unvaccinated individuals to 0.9% in vaccinated ones during a typical season.  This translates to needing to vaccinate 71 healthy adults to prevent one case of flu.

â¢  In a fact box summarizing similar trial data (about 71,000 participants), during a low-spread flu season, vaccination reduces confirmed flu from 2 per 100 unvaccinated adults to 1 per 100 vaccinated adults, protecting 1 in 100 people. 
â¢  Australian health authorities estimate a 50-60% reduction in the likelihood of getting influenza for healthy adults under 65, though this fluctuates yearly based on strain match. 
Reduction in Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Related Impacts

â¢  The same Cochrane review indicates vaccines reduce ILI (symptoms like fever, cough, and muscle aches that may or may not be true flu) by about 16%, from 21.5% to 18.1% risk, meaning 29 adults need vaccination to prevent one ILI case.  This effect is lower because ILI includes non-flu viruses unaffected by the vaccine.

â¢  A randomized trial in healthy working adults (aged 18-64) over two seasons showed that in a year with good vaccine-strain match, vaccination reduced ILI by 34%, physician visits by 42%, and lost workdays by 32%.  In a mismatch year, benefits were not statistically significant.

â¢  CDC data from recent seasons suggest well-matched vaccines can cut flu-related doctor visits by 40-60% across adults, though this includes some with chronic conditions. 

Reduction in Severe Outcomes

â¢  Evidence for hospitalization prevention in healthy adults is limited and uncertain. The Cochrane review found a small potential reduction (from 1.47% to 1.41% risk, or about 0.4% absolute risk reduction), but with wide confidence intervals indicating it may not be meaningful.  No robust data shows impacts on mortality in this group, as flu deaths are rare among young healthy adults.

â¢  For those who still get sick despite vaccination, some studies show reduced severity: vaccinated adults hospitalized with flu had a 26% lower ICU admission risk and 31% lower death risk compared to unvaccinated ones in one analysis, though this pools data across age and health groups. 

Overall, benefits are more pronounced in seasons with good vaccine match and higher flu circulation, but effects are smaller than for high-risk groups like the elderly or children. Vaccines are safe for healthy adults, with mostly mild side effects like arm soreness or low-grade fever, and no strong link to serious harms in trials.  Economic analyses, like the trial in working adults, suggest societal cost savings from reduced absenteeism in good-match years but potential net costs in mismatch years.  While not dramatic for individuals, population-level vaccination helps curb outbreaks.

title: Public trust in the CDC
text:
Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s editorial, “We’re Restoring Public Trust in the CDC,” published in The Wall Street Journal on June 9, 2025, claims the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost public trust due to bureaucratic inertia, politicized science, and mission creep, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

He proposes refocusing the agency on infectious disease, innovation, and transparency. While Kennedy’s call for reform taps into legitimate public skepticism about institutions, his arguments are riddled with inaccuracies, selective data, and misleading assertions that undermine his case. 

Below is a fact-based rebuttal to his editorial, addressing its key claims.

1. Claim: The CDC’s Mission Has Been Corroded by Bureaucratic Inertia and Politicized Science

Kennedy asserts that the CDC’s original mission to protect against infectious disease has been undermined by bureaucracy and politicized science. While no institution is immune to inefficiencies, the CDC’s track record demonstrates consistent advancements in public health. Since its founding in 1946, the CDC has led global efforts in disease surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccine development, contributing to the eradication of smallpox and near-elimination of polio. Life expectancy in the U.S. has risen from 66 years in 1946 to over 78 years today, largely due to public health measures driven by the CDC, including vaccination programs and infectious disease control.

Kennedy’s accusation of “politicized science” lacks specificity and evidence. The CDC operates under rigorous scientific protocols, with advisory committees like the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) composed of independent experts who review data transparently. Kennedy’s own actions—firing all 17 ACIP members in June 2025 and replacing them with individuals, some of whom lack vaccine expertise or have histories of anti-vaccine activism—suggest a move toward ideology-driven decisions rather undercutting his claim of restoring scientific integrity.

2. Claim: COVID Policies Were Irrational and Devastating

Kennedy criticizes CDC policies during COVID-19, including mask mandates, social distancing, school closures, and vaccine recommendations, as irrational and harmful. He cherry-picks examples like “cloth masks on toddlers” and “arbitrary 6-foot distancing” to paint these measures as baseless. However, these policies were grounded in evolving scientific evidence at the time:

â¢ Masks on Young Children: Early in the pandemic, mask mandates for young children were implemented to reduce transmission in settings where social distancing was challenging. Studies, such as a 2021 MMWR report, showed masks reduced COVID-19 transmission in schools by 35-50%. While toddler masking was controversial, it was based on precautionary principles to protect vulnerable populations during a novel pandemic.

â¢ Six-Foot Distancing: The 6-foot guideline was based on early evidence about respiratory droplet spread, as documented in 2020 WHO and CDC reports. While later studies refined this understanding, the guidance was a reasonable interim measure given the urgency and uncertainty.

â¢ School Closures: Kennedy ignores the context of early 2020, when little was known about COVID-19’s impact on children. School closures were implemented globally, not just in the U.S., to curb community spread. A 2020 Lancet study estimated that school closures reduced transmission by 40-60% in some settings. Prolonged closures were contentious, but the CDC issued reopening guidelines as early as February 2021, balancing safety and education.

â¢ Lockdowns: Kennedy’s claim of “economy-crushing lockdowns” oversimplifies a complex issue. Lockdowns varied by state, and the CDC’s role was advisory, not mandatory. A 2021 Nature study found that early lockdowns reduced mortality by 10-20% in high-income countries. Economic impacts were significant but attributing them solely to the CDC ignores state-level policies and global trends.

â¢ Suppression of Therapeutics: Kennedy’s assertion that the CDC suppressed low-cost therapeutics like ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine is misleading. Multiple randomized controlled trials, including those published in NEJM (2021) and JAMA (2022), found no significant benefit from these drugs for COVID-19 treatment or prevention. 

The proposed six aims reflect a desire to streamline the CDC and restore its credibility, but they lack specificity, risk oversimplifying complex issues, and may introduce new challenges. Narrowing the CDC’s focus to infectious diseases could weaken its ability to address interconnected health threats, while vague promises of modernization and workforce investment require detailed plans and funding. The critique of past COVID-19 policies cherry-picks controversial measures without acknowledging their evidence base, potentially undermining trust rather than rebuilding it. A balanced approach would strengthen the CDC’s core mission while preserving its role in addressing chronic diseases and global health threats, with transparent, evidence-based reforms to restore public confidence.

No one in the scientific community currently thinks that under RFK's leadership, trust will be restored in Public Health.  This is a cynical, self-serving ideological platform. Just listen to the respected experts departing the agencies, dismissing them as disgruntled bureaucrats is simply not true.

title: Political philosophy and liberal democracy
text:
Patrick J. Deneen, a political philosopher and professor at the University of Notre Dame, wrote Why Liberalism Failed (2018) and Regime Change: Toward a Postliberal Future (2023).  Attached is an excellent podcast on Freakonomics Radio. He is an important voice in that he is influential in the Trump administration; some have called him the puppet master for MAGA - DOGE. Deneen views JD Vance as the inheritor of this movement, which he views as transformational!

Below I will examine his arguments and a rebuttal to them.  Caution: these ideas are nerdy and a bit theoretical. The tension is between the individual good vs. the community good, and how and where does religion (Christian in Deneen's case or other) stand?

The core thesis posits that classical liberalism—rooted in Enlightenment ideals of individual liberty, progress, and the overthrow of hereditary aristocracy—has paradoxically succeeded in creating a new, exploitative ruling class while eroding the social foundations that once supported ordinary people. Deneen argues that liberalism’s promise of self-determination and merit-based advancement has devolved into a “meritocracy” that benefits an elite minority (the “few”) at the expense of the working-class majority (the “many”), leading to widespread cultural, economic, and political crises across Western democracies.

At the heart of Deneen’s analysis is the distinction between premodern and modern conceptions of liberty. Drawing on classical thinkers like Plato, Aristotle, and the biblical tradition, he contrasts the ancient ideal of liberty as self-rule through virtue, discipline, and communal institutions (e.g., family, church, and local associations) with liberalism’s “negative” liberty, which emphasizes liberation from traditional constraints. Liberalism, he claims, deliberately dismantled these “guardrails”—viewing them as oppressive customs—to enable individual self-creation and progress. However, this flattening of society has created a “vast and widening playground” for the ambitious elite, who thrive in a borderless, technocratic world of global cities, credentialism, and consumption. 

Meanwhile, the masses suffer from institutional decay: weakened families, atomized communities, economic precarity, and cultural dislocation. This divide manifests in a vicious political cycle, where populist resentment (e.g., from working-class voters) clashes with elite disdain, as seen in figures like Donald Trump or Bernie Sanders challenging the status quo. 
Deneen traces this outcome to liberalism’s internal contradictions. Early liberals like John Stuart Mill celebrated “experiments in living” and rejected custom as despotic, but this ignored how traditions protected the vulnerable from elite rapaciousness, as noted by Alexis de Tocqueville and G.K. Chesterton. 

The result is a bifurcated society: elites internalize privatized norms (e.g., delayed family formation enabled by wealth) while condemning “traditional” values as backward, leaving the non-elite without safety nets. This “new class war,” as Deneen borrows from Michael Lind, transcends race and ethnicity, potentially uniting a multiracial working class against managerial elites, though progressive narratives of structural racism obscure this common interest. 

To resolve this, Deneen advocates for “regime change”—not violent revolution, but a “peaceful but vigorous overthrow” of the liberal order through strategic, top-down reformation. He proposes a “postliberal future” grounded in “common-good conservatism,” which revives premodern Aristotelian and Thomistic principles adapted to modern conditions. This “pre-postmodern conservatism” rejects both left-liberal progressivism (with its cultural libertarianism) and right-liberal market individualism, instead envisioning a “mixed constitution” or “aristo populism.” 

Here, a new elite—formed through education in virtue, tradition, and service—would align with populist energies to prioritize the common good: stability, family flourishing, localism, and moral order over endless progress. Practical steps include state interventions to support families, curb markets, integrate elites with non-elites (e.g., through national service), and foster a culture of restraint. Deneen draws on Machiavelli’s realism to argue that this requires “Machiavellian means to Aristotelian ends,” using power pragmatically to rebuild a regime that serves the many, ultimately offering hope beyond liberalism’s failures. 

Critical Rebuttal of Deneen’s Work

While Deneen’s diagnosis of liberalism’s flaws—such as elite detachment and institutional erosion—resonates with observable inequalities, his thesis and prescriptions face substantial critiques on conceptual, practical, and ethical grounds. Critics argue that Regime Change romanticizes a premodern past, underestimates liberalism’s achievements, and risks authoritarianism in its pursuit of a postliberal order.

First, Deneen’s portrayal of liberalism as a monolithic failure ignores its tangible successes in promoting human flourishing. Liberalism has driven unprecedented economic growth, technological advancement, and poverty reduction, lifting billions globally while expanding rights for marginalized groups (e.g., women, minorities, and LGBTQ+ individuals). By framing these as mere elite manipulations, Deneen dismisses how individual liberties have empowered the “many” beyond traditional hierarchies. As reviewer Daniel J. Mahoney notes, this overlooks opportunities to reform liberalism rather than abandon it, turning the book into a “lost opportunity” for nuanced revival of both liberal and conservative traditions. Moreover, his nostalgia for preliberal societies glosses over their oppressions: aristocratic rule often entrenched inequality, religious intolerance, and limited mobility, problems liberalism explicitly addressed. Critics like Matt McManus contend that Deneen’s “illiberal alternative” evokes an “autocratic and aristocratic” vision that could reinstate such hierarchies under the guise of the common good. 

Second, the proposal for regime change is vague and potentially dangerous. Deneen insists on peaceful means, but his invocation of Machiavellian tactics—using power to impose Aristotelian virtues—raises alarms about coercion. How, exactly, would this new elite be formed and installed without descending into tyranny? The book sketches cultural and institutional reforms but lacks a concrete roadmap, as Carl Eric Scott points out, showing “what a conservative revolution could look like, but not how to make it a reality.” This ambiguity could enable reactionary populism, where “aristo populism” empowers demagogues to enforce moral order, eroding democratic pluralism. Samuel Moyn warns that Deneen’s ideas pose “significant danger to liberal democracy,” as they channel anti-elite resentment into a framework that rejects core liberal safeguards like individual rights and separation of powers. 

Third, Deneen’s binary of elites versus masses oversimplifies social dynamics and could exacerbate divisions. His “common-good conservatism” assumes a unified “many” aligned against progressive elites, but this ignores internal conflicts within the working class (e.g., cultural, racial, or economic divides) and the role of liberal institutions in mediating them. Harry Readhead critiques the expanded state role in promoting moral order as potentially invasive, risking the very “progressive tyranny” Deneen decries but from the right.  Furthermore, by labeling liberalism’s progress as deconstructive, Deneen engages in a form of conservative self-deception, as Aaron Ross Powell argues, reproducing populist myths that America needs radical overhaul rather than incremental fixes. 

Overall, while Deneen’s work provokes necessary debate on liberalism’s limits, it risks trading one form of elitism for another, potentially undermining the freedoms it claims to transcend. A more balanced approach might integrate his insights into liberal reforms, rather than pursuing a postliberal rupture that could prove more divisive than redemptive.

Liberalism has driven unprecedented economic growth, technological advancement, and poverty reduction, lifting billions globally while expanding rights for marginalized groups (e.g., women, minorities, and LGBTQ+ individuals). By framing these as mere elite manipulations, Deneen dismisses how individual liberties have empowered the “many” beyond traditional hierarchies. As reviewer Daniel J. Mahoney notes, this overlooks opportunities to reform liberalism rather than abandon it, turning the book into a “lost opportunity” for nuanced revival of both liberal and conservative traditions. Moreover, his nostalgia for preliberal societies glosses over their oppressions: aristocratic rule often entrenched inequality, religious intolerance, and limited mobility, problems liberalism explicitly addressed. Critics like Matt McManus contend that Deneen’s “illiberal alternative” evokes an “autocratic and aristocratic” vision that could reinstate such hierarchies under the guise of the common good. 

Second, the proposal for regime change is vague and potentially dangerous. Deneen insists on peaceful means, but his invocation of Machiavellian tactics—using power to impose Aristotelian virtues—raises alarms about coercion. How, exactly, would this new elite be formed and installed without descending into tyranny? The book sketches cultural and institutional reforms but lacks a concrete roadmap, as Carl Eric Scott points out, showing “what a conservative revolution could look like, but not how to make it a reality.” This ambiguity could enable reactionary populism, where “aristo populism” empowers demagogues to enforce moral order, eroding democratic pluralism. Samuel Moyn warns that Deneen’s ideas pose “significant danger to liberal democracy,” as they channel anti-elite resentment into a framework that rejects core liberal safeguards like individual rights and separation of powers. 

Third, Deneen’s binary of elites versus masses oversimplifies social dynamics and could exacerbate divisions. His “common-good conservatism” assumes a unified “many” aligned against progressive elites, but this ignores internal conflicts within the working class (e.g., cultural, racial, or economic divides) and the role of liberal institutions in mediating them. Harry Readhead critiques the expanded state role in promoting moral order as potentially invasive, risking the very “progressive tyranny” Deneen decries but from the right.  Furthermore, by labeling liberalism’s progress as deconstructive, Deneen engages in a form of conservative self-deception, as Aaron Ross Powell argues, reproducing populist myths that America needs radical overhaul rather than incremental fixes. 

Overall, while Deneen’s work provokes necessary debate on liberalism’s limits, it risks trading one form of elitism for another, potentially undermining the freedoms it claims to transcend. A more balanced approach might integrate his insights into liberal reforms, rather than pursuing a postliberal rupture that could prove more divisive than redemptive.

title: Everyday uses of AI
text:
I don't wish to "over-hype" AI, but it is happening! Here is a simple primer for applications you might consider in your current life!  Within the past 6 mos., I have completely embraced any one of the AI engines (ChatGPT or grok most often, but also Perplexity, Gemini) for a variety of initial conversations or explorations of topics. For travel, it has become a game-changer. As a language translator it is on point now.  Initial foray into new topics or providing balanced or pro/cons on controversial issues has been outstanding. As a medical resource, I have been impressed by the sensibility that it presents. It does take some playing around to craft a focused request to be maximally responsive and consider it to be iterative to refine a conversation, as you may with a travel agent, a lawyer, a financial advisor, or a doctor. And for fun, uploading images for identification, etc.

At present, it is simply providing textual responses. The next level will require it to perform additional actions (i.e. agentic AI). In addition to providing information and resources, actually make reservations or purchases, linked to your account after you give approval.

Of course, buyer beware in that you are responsible for double-checking everything, asking for references for everything, etc. However, I have generally been impressed at the accuracy with these queries. Over time, these will become so embedded into our phones (and other devices) that they will be in the background (and we wouldn't have to make as much hype about it). Much like "google maps", rarely do I need to cross-check it for accuracy. Similar to many tools people come to rely on (i.e. pilots using various navigational or other instruments, physicians using test results, electricians using meters), although you do need a "common sense" about you!

title: Medicaid policy and access to care
text:
OK, you could see this coming from a mile away! This will engender much fear, anger, and resistance from many people. But let me say that I generally support this concept (of course with checks and balances). 

We all know that health care is too expensive, our current spend of 18-20% of GDP is unsustainable for the outcomes we have. Both sides of the aisle would agree with that. There is legitimate waste in the system, perhaps some fraud as well. We have a 3-legged stool of providers (health systems and physicians), insurers (private employer/insurer or gov't), and patients that carefully do a dance, everyone being unhappy. The whole concept of "prior authorization" (PA) to limit "needless" care (testing as well as procedures) along with preferred network alliances has been at play to limit the spend. Private insurers have long utilized PA by using a variety of guidelines, rules, and data to decide what will be covered or paid for (through internal review and oversight by "independent" physicians employed by the insurer), many times at odds with the treating physician as to the medical necessity.  The complexity and volume of ever-changing guidelines is such that algorithms and AI models have been legitimately used by private insurers (both in commercial as well as Medicare advantage plans), perhaps with lesser oversight by individual physicians.

Many of the decisions for medical necessity are pretty straight-forward and lend themselves to an algorithmic framework to approve or deny based on solid guidance from the literature. Such denials are necessary, they balance incentives, and doing so efficiently using AI is a good thing.  But we all agree on the need for expert physician oversight, periodic reviews, etc.

So, what is new? Well, traditional Medicare (with private supplemental plans) has been shielded from much of the prior authorization process, unlike Medicare Advantage plans (now over 50% Medicare folks are on these) or commercial insurance.  What is being rolled out by CMS now is a 6-year pilot program for traditional Medicare in 6 states (New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona and Washington), involving certain targeted higher cost medical interventions noted below:

Here's a full list of the procedures that will be included in the pilot program: 

Electrical Nerve Stimulators 

Sacral Nerve Stimulation for Urinary Incontinence 

Phrenic Nerve Stimulator 

Deep Brain Stimulation for Essential Tremor and Parkinson's Disease 

Vagus Nerve Stimulation 

Induced Lesions of Nerve Tracts 

Epidural Steroid Injections for Pain Management excluding facet joint injections 

Percutaneous Vertebral Augmentation (PVA) for Vertebral Compression Fracture (VCF) 

Cervical Fusion 

Arthroscopic Lavage and Arthroscopic Debridement for the Osteoarthritic Knee 

Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea 

Incontinence Control Devices 

Diagnosis and Treatment of Impotence 

Percutaneous Image-Guided Lumbar Decompression for Spinal Stenosis 

Skin and Tissue Substitutes —only applicable to MAC jurisdictions and states that have an active LCD in place

What is common to this list: 
1. procedural, new technologies, more complex and proprietary. 
2. less competition, performed at tertiary centers, therefore most expensive (c/w alternatives). 
3. Being newer, limited data and experience re. utility, cost-effectiveness c/w alternatives in a real-world large population setting. Therefore, more prone to disagreement amongst experts as to necessity!
4. In US healthcare system, we push the envelope and innovate newer therapies and mousetraps.

I suspect there will be vigorous pushback and politics behind this! Arguing this is privatization of Medicare, etc. And about utilizing AI in the prior auth process. 

I welcome discussion on this.

title: Mental health and AI companions
text:
Mental health is relevant to every one of us. There is a lot of appropriate focus on this, from the earlier Prozac-era to the iPhone internet social media era, and most recently to the AI-chatbot era. There are special issues for children, for parents, and everyone.  The speed, personalization, and remarkable efficiency of the large language models (LLMs) are creating both hope and unintended consequences. How to harness the benefits safely and avoid the harm is tricky, is not clear, and will evolve.

Recent reports have identified incidents of suicides (one recent case of murder), where the individual actively chatted about their ideation with these LLMs (attached article notes the first lawsuit against an AI company). Psychiatric consultants have been advising these companies on how best to adjust the algorithms in this era. We may all have our own knee-jerk opinions, but we should seek out data-driven best practices. Our gut reaction of outrage maybe directed towards modernity, technology, big corporation greed to foster addictive potential, as well as parenting shortfalls. 

The issue of chatbots amplifying pre-existing mental illness is an important concern, by feeding into paranoia and bizarre hallucinations as bots have a tendency to be sycophantic and ingratiating! Specific features such as keeping the “memory” function on may contribute to this. 

One obvious area is for children, as to how to balance "privacy" issues and escalating to inform parents of any red flags. Current models do flag many warnings and redirect to existing resources on mental health and suicide prevention. These LLMs shine in their capacity to engage in confidence, for individuals who may not wish to share with real people. Indeed, there are other non-AI means to search the web for information and banning these tools is not the solution or possible. Using targeted and well-thought-out alerting systems to escalate and bring in a human professional therapist is perhaps the best approach. Let's say such a resource is made available via an LLM, will the user continue to engage, even if it is offered free of charge? 

At present, we all need to be aware and pay attention to this space. I do not know what the right answer is. Open to further discussion on this sensitive topic.  The issue of AI in all aspects of our existence will generate countless discussions.

title: MAHA and the politics of public health
text:
The idea behind MAHA (“Make America Healthy Again”) highlights real problems — chronic disease, unhealthy diets, and a profit-driven health system. But under Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the movement hasn’t tackled these issues meaningfully. Instead, he’s cut nearly $500 million in mRNA research funding, jeopardizing lifesaving work. The piece asks how U.S. politics shifted from Trump’s Operation Warp Speed, a major pandemic success, to Kennedy dismantling it. It also points to ongoing reporting and analysis on what MAHA means for public health and politics.

There is an excellent discussion of the lessons from the Covid-19 era, esp. the messaging, politics on both sides, and how RFK came to be. He is best understood as an anti-pollution environmental guy, who has extended that to anything put in the body from meds to vaccines to corporations that produce them to conspiracies. 

As an aside, I found reference to a book that resonated for me: The Wizard and the Prophet: Two Remarkable Scientists and Their Dueling Visions to Shape Tomorrow’s World # by Charles C. Mann.

Central theme: Mann contrasts two archetypes for confronting environmental and societal challenges:

“Wizards” (techno-optimists) who argue that innovation and growth—exemplified by agronomist Norman Borlaug—can solve problems like food, water, energy, and climate.

“Prophets” (limits-to-growth) who, following ecologist William Vogt, contend that technology often is the problem and that we must reduce consumption and live within ecological boundaries.
He applies these lenses to four domains: food, water, energy, and climate, showing how the two mindsets clash and sometimes complement each other.

Those contrasting approaches are a great framework to understand potential solutions for the future in a variety of areas!
